articles.full_text:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump's chief economic adviser called on former Federal Reserve Chair Jerome Powell to leave the central bank's board after an internal report cited management failures in the renovation of its headquarters.
Most Read from Bloomberg
- Manchester City Verdict Strains UK-UAE Diplomatic Relations
- Rodman Joins Trump as He Eyes Meeting With North Korea's Kim
- Larry Ellison Risk Exposed by Paramount and Oracle Debt Binges
- FlyDubai's Perilous Plunge and Survival Puts Focus on Jet Design
- Lula, Bolsonaro in Tight Race as Brazil Prepares to Vote
"I think that it's time for him to move on and to respect the independence of the Fed," Kevin Hassett, head of the National Economic Council at the White House, said on Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures when asked whether Powell should resign.
The Fed's internal watchdog said in a Sept. 30 report it found no evidence of criminal wrongdoing and didn't identify any "administrative misconduct" connected to the $2.4 billion renovation project in Washington, but cited management deficiencies that helped almost double the project's original cost.
Trump responded with a social post saying Powell, whom he relentlessly pressured to lower interest rates as Fed chair, "should be forced to resign from the Board."
US Attorney General Todd Blanche, whom Trump has asked to review the Fed inspector general's report, said in an interview Friday that the Justice Department wouldn't reopen a criminal investigation of Powell based on the findings.
The Fed has said it will engage an independent auditor to scrutinize the building costs. Blanche added that if that review finds any evidence of criminal wrongdoing, the Justice Department could investigate.
"I expect there will be an auditing process," Blanche said. "If they learn anything that rises to any kind of criminal misconduct, you better believe we're going to investigate that."
Powell has been on the Fed's board of governors since leaving his position as chair in May, breaking with the precedent of Fed chairs' leaving the central bank when their leadership term ends.
Powell has said that threats of criminal investigations into him and the Federal Reserve left him with no option but to stay, a stance that Trump and other members of his administration condemned.
While Trump has long pressed the Fed to lower borrowing costs, policymakers under Chairman Kevin Warsh last month voted unanimously to raise interest rates by a quarter percentage point in the face of stubborn inflation.
"As you saw, that Chairman Warsh voted with people to increase interest rates," Hassett told Fox News. "I disagree with that decision, but we respect that he was doing that for the right reasons."

articles.title: AUD/USD Forecast: Australia's Next Inflation Report Will Test Westpac's Outlook - Exchange Rates UK
articles.summary: AUD/USD Forecast: Australia's Next Inflation Report Will Test Westpac's Outlook  Exchange Rates UK
articles.full_text:
FX strategists at Westpac still expect a November RBA hike, but Goldman Sachs and Rabobank favour patience, leaving AUD/USD sensitive to the next inflation report.
Australia's softer-than-expected underlying inflation has weakened market bets on another November interest-rate rise without shifting Westpac's forecast, exposing a disagreement that matters for the Australian Dollar.
August's trimmed-mean inflation of 0.2% on the month and 3.6% annually matched Westpac's expectations and remains consistent with its forecast for a 0.9% quarterly rise in the third quarter.
Goldman Sachs expects an extended pause, while Rabobank believes any further tightening is more likely to wait until early 2027.
AUD/USD closed Friday, 2 October, near US$0.6957, up 0.40% on the day, after losing 3.15% in September.
The recovery accompanied a broader Dollar decline following the weaker-than-expected US jobs report, which reduced the immediate pressure for another Federal Reserve hike.
Markets cut November odds, but Westpac holds its call
Westpac's 1 October Morning Report recorded a clear change in Australian rate expectations after the CPI release.
"Following a slight downside surprise on inflation figures yesterday, near-term pricing for the RBA has recalibrated, with a follow-up rate hike in November now seen as a circa 25% chance versus a circa 40% chance previously."
Those are the report's dated market probabilities, rather than Westpac's own forecast.
Its economists saw little reason to alter their inflation projections.
"In Australia, the August CPI was spot on Westpac's forecast, with headline inflation up 0.4%mth/4.0%yr and trimmed mean inflation up 0.2%mth/3.6%yr, though the latter was slightly below market expectations."
The softer surprise should not be confused with falling annual headline inflation, which rose to 4.0% from July's 3.5%, while the annual trimmed mean was unchanged.
In its analysis of the latest CPI figures, Westpac analysts retained its November hike call, warning that businesses passing on higher energy costs posed upside risks to underlying inflation later this year.
Its 0.9% third-quarter trimmed-mean forecast would represent an acceleration from 0.8% in the second quarter.
How much restraint is already in place?
The RBA's September increase took the cash rate to 4.60%, following a cumulative percentage point of tightening during 2026.
The disagreement centres on whether those increases need more time to restrain demand or whether persistent inflation requires another move in November.
Goldman's assessment after the September decision favoured waiting.
"Our base case is that the RBA holds policy for an extended period until a gradual easing cycle commences from 2H2027."
That means cuts starting in the second half of next year, although Goldman still regarded further tightening as a material risk, including in November if inflation surprised higher.
Rabobank's October outlook gives greater weight to the danger of excessive restraint.
"While we do not rule out the possibility of further rate hikes, we think the RBA is going to be feeling its way and will be careful that any further tightening does not tip the economy into recession or cause a disorderly spike in the unemployment rate."
The bank highlighted weaker new-home construction inflation and a 0.4% monthly fall in market services prices excluding volatile items.
"Overall, we believe that the August inflation data supports our view that the RBA will not be in a rush to raise the cash rate in November and that any further lift in the cash rate is likely to be delayed until early next year."
For AUD/USD, fewer expected Australian hikes remove one potential source of yield support, although Friday's rally shows how weaker US data can offset that pressure.
The next Australian CPI release on 28 October will include September-quarter figures, allowing investors to test Westpac's 0.9% forecast before the November decision.

articles.title: Fed Must Decide on Rates This Month Without the Data It Normally Uses - Startup Fortune
articles.summary: Fed Must Decide on Rates This Month Without the Data It Normally Uses  Startup Fortune
articles.full_text:
The Fed still has its September jobs report before the October 27-28 meeting, but a soft payroll print and an inflation report due October 14 have left traders arguing over whether September's hike was the start of another tightening leg or a one-off.
The Bureau of Labor Statistics released September's jobs report on October 2, showing employers added 29,000 jobs while the unemployment rate ticked higher. The consumer price index for September is scheduled for October 14, and September retail sales are scheduled for October 15. Congress passed a stopgap funding bill in September. It keeps federal agencies funded through December 11. So the shutdown risk hanging over markets earlier in the cycle is no longer the reason traders are struggling with the October decision.
That still leaves the timing unusually tight. The Federal Reserve meets on October 27 and 28 to decide what to do with interest rates: one weak payroll report is already in hand, and the next inflation print lands less than two weeks before the vote.
That's not a small setup. The Fed's current chair, Kevin Warsh, has been trying to keep inflation expectations pinned down after September's quarter-point hike, while the labor market is sending mixed signals. ADP's private payroll count showed the economy lost 32,000 private-sector jobs in September, with construction down 5,000 and manufacturing down 2,000. The official BLS report was softer than expected too, with 29,000 jobs added and downward revisions to the prior two months.
Here's the part that makes the October meeting different from the ones before it. The Fed raised rates on September 16, lifting the target range to 3.75%-4.00%, its first increase in three years. Since then, prediction markets have leaned toward another hike before year-end, though contracts tied specifically to the October meeting have recently favored no change over an immediate follow-up move.
Futures traders have flipped from pricing rate cuts to giving a September Fed rate hike roughly a coin-flip chance, after Fed Chair Kevin Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole speech and a blowout August jobs report. A US-Iran oil shock pushing Brent above $100 a barrel is adding to the inflation pressure, and Treasury yields have jumped to multi-month... - fed rate hike probability september 2026 - kevin warsh federal reserve policy shift
Frankly, a market that has moved from expecting cuts to debating another hike in the span of a year is unusual on its own. Add in a weak payroll print, still-elevated inflation, and an election calendar sitting just beyond the meeting, and you get a setup where nobody has a clean read on where policy lands next.
Not every market participant is spooked. The index closed out the week ending October 3 up 1.1%, and the Nasdaq-100 gained 1.2% over the same stretch, so stocks have largely absorbed the September hike and the soft jobs report. UBS, separately, has argued that markets are pricing in too much tightening. That forecast sits uneasily next to prediction-market odds for another hike before year-end, and it underlines just how unsettled the professional read on this has become.
Bulls are buying stocks. Rate traders are arguing about how far the Fed can tighten. That disconnect is the real story for anyone running a company whose fundraising, debt costs, or runway depends on where rates land in five weeks. Founders in rate-sensitive sectors, real estate, fintech lenders, anything borrowed-against, are watching a decision get made with the labor market slowing and inflation still uncomfortably sticky.
There is still one CPI print to check that against, and it lands on October 14.
The committee will set a rate touching every mortgage, loan, and credit line with a soft jobs report, one more CPI print, private payroll data, surveys, and anecdotal reads all pulling on the decision at once.

The BSE Sensex fell 570.59 points, or 0.79%, to close at 71,909.70. During the session, the 30-stock index plunged as much as 1,187.41 points to touch a fresh 52-week low of 71,292.88. Meanwhile, the NSE Nifty 50 dropped 198.50 points, or 0.88%, to settle at 22,421.95.
GIFT Nifty ended 0.59% or 133.50 points up, closed the session at 22,624.50 on 2 October.
Sensex closed at 71,909.70, down by 570.59 points (-0.79%), extending the recent weakness amid continued selling pressure. The index also breached the April 2025 swing low of 71,425.01 during the session before recovering and closing above that level.
On the Sensex outlook, Sachin Gupta, VP – Technical Research at Choice Equity Broking Private Limited, said, “On the daily chart, the index remains below the 50-Day EMA at 75,544.56 and 200-Day EMA at 77,684.60, while RSI has slipped to 24.55, indicating deeply oversold momentum. The broader support zone is placed at 71,000–71,200, while resistance is at 72,300–72,500.”
Meanwhile, on the Nifty 50 outlook, Ajit Mishra, SVP – Research, Religare Broking, said that the index corrected sharply after declining for eight successive weeks and tested the key long-term moving-average support zone comprising the 200-WSMA and 200-WEMA around 22,400-22,600, a zone revisited after nearly six years. The index also moved closer to the previous major swing low of 22,182.55 before closing at 22,421.95.
“While the broader trend remains negative, the combination of key technical supports and oversold conditions could trigger a near-term rebound. Participants may adopt a hedged approach, with 22,800 as the initial upside target, followed by 23,100-23,200. A decisive break below the April low could negate the rebound possibility and drag the index towards 21,700-22,000. Hence, appropriate stop-losses and disciplined risk management remain important,” Mishra said.
US stocks ended higher on Friday, with weaker-than-expected jobs data reducing expectations of a Federal Reserve rate hike at its policy meeting later this month.
The Nasdaq Composite advanced 319.27 points, or 1.2%, to close at 27,190.86. The index touched a record high during the session before paring gains as Treasury yields reversed direction. For the week, the index posted a gain of 0.6%, marking its third consecutive weekly advance.
S&P 500
The S&P 500 rose 56.27 points, or 0.7%, to 7,722.72. Despite Friday’s gains, the index slipped 0.3% over the week.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 250 points, or 0.5%, to finish at 51,176.46. The index ended the week about 1.3% lower.
South Korean equities closed the September 28-October 2 week in the red despite a strong recovery towards the end of the period. The Kospi fell 77.18 points, or 1.1%, from the previous week to end at 7,003.74, as gains in major semiconductor stocks were insufficient to offset the sharp losses recorded earlier in the week.
The benchmark index started the week with a steep 2.7% decline to 6,889.74 on September 28, ending a four-session winning streak as investors booked profits in large-cap technology stocks. Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix faced significant selling pressure, while rising US Treasury yields and ongoing uncertainty over the Middle East further dampened investor sentiment.
Japanese equities ended lower on Friday, dragged down by declines across the Paper & Pulp, Transport and Communication sectors.
The Nikkei 225 fell 0.87% by the close in Tokyo. Among the top performers on the index, Resonac Holdings Corp (TYO:4004) gained 8.71%, or 1,385 points, to finish the session at 17,280.
Taiwan’s benchmark TAIEX index rose 122 points, or 0.3%, to end Friday’s session at a fresh record high of 48,476. The index extended its gains for a third straight session, supported primarily by advances in energy minerals, producer manufacturing and process industry stocks.

articles.title: This is how the informal market closes in Cuba: The dollar and euro end the day on a high note - CiberCuba
articles.summary: This is how the informal market closes in Cuba: The dollar and euro end the day on a high note  CiberCuba
articles.full_text:
At 8:00 PM, local Cuban time, closes the day this Saturday, October 3, 2026, with the dollar and the euro on the rise compared to the previous day. The Cuban peso continues to lose ground against the two main cash currencies, while the MLC experiences a significant decline, although its quotation should be viewed with caution due to the limited volume of operations supporting it.
The U.S. dollar is trading at 785 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of this trading day. This represents an increase of 5.5 pesos compared to the previous session, when the average value was at 780 CUP. In a weekly perspective, the U.S. currency has risen by 47.5 pesos from the 738 CUP recorded seven days ago, equating to an increase of 6.4%. Over the last month, the dollar has gained 102.5 pesos from the 683 CUP recorded 30 days ago, although this 30-day comparison may partially reflect methodological adjustments in the index and not just market movements. Today, the dollar hits its highest point in the last 30 days, with a ceiling of 785 CUP and a floor of 683 CUP during that period. It continues to set the tone for the informal market in a context of structural currency shortages.
The euro is quoted at 885 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of this trading day. This represents an increase of 7 pesos compared to the previous day, when the average value was at 878 CUP. Over the last week, the European currency has risen 45.5 pesos from the 840 CUP recorded seven days ago, reflecting a 5.4% increase. In the last month, it has accumulated a gain of 112.5 pesos from the 773 CUP of 30 days ago, although this comparison should be interpreted with caution due to potential methodological adjustments of the index. Today, the euro reaches its highest point in the last 30 days, ranging between 773 and 885 CUP during that period. It surpasses the dollar by 100 pesos, solidifying its dominant position in the Cuban parallel market.
The MLC is quoted tentatively at 460 Cuban pesos (CUP) at the close of this trading session, a figure that should be taken with caution due to the low volume of operations backing it. This represents a decline of 25.5 pesos compared to the previous day, when the average value was 486 CUP. In the last week, it has decreased by 24.5 pesos from the 485 CUP recorded seven days ago, and in the last month, it has accumulated a loss of 49 pesos from the 509 CUP of 30 days ago. Its peak in the last 30 days was 547 CUP, while its minimum was 415 CUP. Without physical existence, its use is limited to state-run businesses that accept it, which restricts its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Exchange Rate Evolution
- Exchange rate of the dollar USD to CUP: 785 CUP.
- Exchange rate of the euro EUR to CUP: 885 CUP.
- Exchange rate from MLC to CUP: 460 CUP (indicative value, limited data).
The official exchange rate of the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III), at 695 CUP per dollar and 783 CUP per euro, remains well below the values that prevail in everyday practice in the informal currency market.
Although Segment III was introduced as a more flexible exchange mechanism, its official rate remains far from that of the informal market and fails to meet the actual demand for foreign currency from the population. The gap between the official dollar rate (695 CUP) and the informal rate (785 CUP) exceeds 90 pesos; in the case of the euro, the difference between the official rate of 783 CUP and the 885 CUP in the parallel market is nearly 102 pesos.
In a scenario of sustained inflation, low state wages, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, every fluctuation in the informal market directly impacts internal prices and the purchasing power of Cubans.
The Exchange Rate of CiberCuba is an index of the informal Cuban market created through the automated analysis of thousands of currency buying and selling posts in Telegram and Facebook groups. The calculation disregards atypical offers and spam messages, weighs each transaction based on its age, and consolidates a representative value that is updated several times a day.

articles.title: Howard Marks: The 30-Year Treasury at 5.5% Isn't a Crisis, It's an Invoice - finance.biggo.com
articles.summary: Howard Marks: The 30-Year Treasury at 5.5% Isn't a Crisis, It's an Invoice  finance.biggo.com
articles.full_text:
When the US 30-year Treasury yield closed above 5.3% in August — a 19-year high — the Treasury's response was to double its long-dated bond buybacks and signal it would do "whatever it takes" to push borrowing costs down. Stanley Druckenmiller — the investor who hired and mentored a young Scott Bessent at Soros Fund Management and ran the firm's landmark 1992 bet against the British pound — watched and offered a four-line diagnosis in a late-August Wall Street Journal op-ed that Howard Marks, speaking on The Memo by Howard Marks, considers definitive: "Every basis point of artificial yield suppression is a subsidy to procrastination. Whatever this operation saves in basis points, it will cost multiples in delay."
The market, Marks notes, rendered its own verdict almost immediately. Long rates fell for a day, then bounced back. When the Treasury tripled the buyback size to $6 billion in early September, yields moved higher anyway. An Evercore ISI note at the time described the "big reveal" of the ramped-up operation — and noted that rates went up, not down, at the moment of writing.
The market's verdict has only hardened since. In the final days of September, the 30-year yield pushed through 5.5% and reached 5.64% on September 30 — well above the 5.31% August peak that prompted the buyback campaign — before trading at 5.61% on October 1, according to Treasury data. The 5.5% level that Druckenmiller described as the price of attracting buyers is no longer hypothetical.
The reason, Marks argues, is that buybacks respond to the effects of rising rates rather than the underlying causes. His ice-pack analogy cuts to the heart of it: "Forcing rates down by buying bonds is like a doctor applying an ice pack to a patient with a fever. The ice pack may lower the patient's temperature, but the patient isn't likely to get healthy until the underlying cause of the fever has been dealt with."
What's actually pushing long rates up
Marks identifies four distinct forces, none of which Treasury buybacks address.
| Root cause | The specifics | 
|---|---|
| Stubborn inflation | PCE inflation at 3.7% in July 2026, against the Fed's 2% target | 
| Oil price shock | Elevated prices tied to the Iran conflict; bond buyers demand inflation protection | 
| Fiscal indiscipline | Deficit near 6% of GDP with only 4% unemployment; net interest outlays above $1 trillion this year, exceeding the defense budget | 
| Capital demand from AI | McKinsey estimates over $5 trillion in AI-related data center spending through 2030 | 
The AI point deserves particular attention. Even equity-financed spending competes for the same pool of available capital, which means bonds must pay more to attract investors. Meanwhile, the Treasury must refinance maturing debt and issue roughly $2 trillion in new paper each year. The market is being asked to absorb more supply at the same moment it has more alternatives.
Those alternatives increasingly include not holding Treasuries at all. Foreign investors own roughly $9.2 trillion of Treasury securities, but the buyer base has been thinning. Japan, the largest foreign holder, held $1.10 trillion in July, down from a February peak of $1.24 trillion. Mainland China's holdings slid to $618 billion, less than half their 2013 peak, as Beijing continues a long retreat. Foreign official holdings — the category that captures central banks and sovereign funds — fell from $4.01 trillion in February to $3.77 trillion in July.
| Major foreign holders of US Treasuries | July 2026 | Change vs. July 2025 | 
|---|---|---|
| Japan | $1,104B | -$52B | 
| United Kingdom | $998B | +$102B | 
| China (mainland) | $618B | -$78B | 
| Taiwan | $296B | -$13B | 
Marks directly contradicts Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's claim — reported by the Financial Times in August — that yields don't reflect fundamentals. "On the contrary, I think U.S. long-term bond yields are reflecting the fundamentals as just described," he stated on the podcast.
The structural flaw in the buyback plan
Treasury buybacks are financed through general cash resources, which are ultimately replenished through additional issuance. If long-bond buybacks are paired with greater T-bill issuance, overall indebtedness doesn't change — but the maturity profile shortens. The US government would then need to refinance more frequently at whatever rates prevail. That, Marks says, "doesn't seem likely to bolster confidence in our fiscal picture."
Druckenmiller's broader point, which Marks amplifies, is that markets ultimately clear at the price fundamentals demand. If the 30-year must trade at 5.5% to attract buyers, "that isn't a crisis. It is an invoice. We either must pay it, whatever it grows to, or we must fix the underlying problem."
That's a reframing worth sitting with. The bond market isn't punishing the US out of spite. It's pricing what the country's fiscal choices actually cost.
Weimar, the dollar, and the goat problem
Marks has a personal connection to currency debasement. As a young man, he owned a Weimar Republic 1,000-mark note overprinted to one million marks. His framing of what that meant, delivered on the podcast: "You can easily turn a 1,000-mark note into a 1,000,000-mark note, but it's likely to still buy just one goat."
The debasement trade — paying debts in dollars of reduced purchasing power — is the risk Marks flagged as far back as his 2008 memo "The Limits to Negativism." He's careful, though, to note that his 2008 fear that Fed balance-sheet expansion would debase the dollar or accelerate inflation proved wrong; that expansion largely offset the destruction of money and credit from the financial crisis. Today's deficit financing is different. It occurs during prosperity, responds to deficits of our own making, and can genuinely add to aggregate demand and inflation pressure.
On the dollar's reserve status, Marks is skeptical of near-term alternatives. The dollar was involved in 89% of foreign exchange transactions in 2025 and accounted for 57% of allocated official reserves in Q1 2026. The euro remains second but hasn't closed the gap. The renminbi sits at roughly 2% of allocated reserves, with capital controls and geopolitical tensions making rapid ascent unlikely. A MUFG Bank note from mid-September observed that gold's market value had recently surpassed foreign official holdings of US Treasury securities as the world's largest reserve asset — a notable shift, but not yet a replacement. Federal Reserve researchers pushed back on that framing in a September 3 note, arguing the crossover mostly reflects a gold-price surge driven by private-sector demand and valuation gains on legacy holdings, and that by June 2026 foreign official Treasury holdings had again moved ahead of gold in dollar terms. "For the most part, the world is probably stuck with the dollar for now," Marks concluded.
Warren Buffett's warning at the May 2025 Berkshire Hathaway meeting provides the capstone: "Fiscal policy is what scares me in the United States. We're operating at a fiscal deficit now that is unsustainable over a very long period of time. We don't know whether that means two years or twenty years, because there's never been a country like the United States."
The loop at the bottom is the problem. Buybacks push prices up briefly, but the fundamental forces reassert themselves.
What a real fix would look like
Marks is explicit that an acute crisis — a failed auction or buyer's strike — seems improbable. But he argues the chronic cost is already being imposed. His solution set has five components, and it's uncomfortable for everyone:
- Accept that debt will likely never be lower than today; stop talking about "paying it down"
- Adopt fiscal responsibility as an actual priority, not a slogan
- Raise revenue through higher income tax rates, especially at the top end, and eliminate tax preferences
- Hold spending growth below GDP growth
- Boost productivity growth through AI adoption and pro-business policies
The crucial condition: added revenue must not simply be spent. If these steps were taken, annual deficits would shrink as a percentage of GDP and the debt-to-GDP ratio could decline. Marks concedes "no one likes to pay higher taxes" — but for a country unwilling to cut spending, "I sincerely doubt there's another solution available."
Why selling US stocks isn't the answer
Marks recounts a question from a friend — a nationally known entrepreneur, not an investment professional — who asked last month whether to sell his stocks. His answer was no.
The logic is worth walking through carefully. If you sell US stocks and put the money in a bank, a money market fund, or bonds denominated in dollars, you haven't escaped the risk at all. To actually act on concerns about dollar debasement, you'd need to move into non-dollar currencies, gold, non-US real estate, non-US companies, or cryptocurrencies. Each carries its own set of problems. Many developed-world companies have poorer growth prospects and heavier regulation than their US counterparts. Emerging-market companies may look attractive, but realizing that potential is far more uncertain.
Marks lists what has drawn institutional investors to the US for decades — free markets, pro-business climate, innovation, rule of law, capital markets — and says those qualities "largely remain intact." No other country possesses them to the same extent. He also notes that other nations run deficits too; moving into another currency subject to debasement accomplishes little.
This creates an uncomfortable position that Marks acknowledges honestly: he identifies a genuine, chronic, arithmetic problem while concluding that the obvious portfolio response is probably wrong. Acting early "could easily look like a big mistake for a very long time." The reckoning may be far off. The timing is unknowable.
The same arithmetic, closer to home
Marks's argument is addressed to American readers, but the bonds at its center are held worldwide, and Asia'

articles.title: Why U.S. airlines balked at adopting Boeing’s latest 737 Max software versions - The Air Current
articles.summary: Why U.S. airlines balked at adopting Boeing’s latest 737 Max software versions  The Air CurrentUS FAA says Boeing 737 MAX software glitch poses no safety issue  ReutersFAA says Boeing 737 Max software glitch not a flight-safety issue  CNBCUS regulator details missed-approach conditions that could affect 737 vertical navigation  flightglobal.comBoeing 737 MAX Glitch Has No Impact: Akasa  Rediff
articles.full_text:
Log-in here if you’re already a subscriber
Air safety reporting is made accessible without a subscription as a public service. Subscribe to The Air Current for full access to our scoops, in-depth reporting and industry analysis.
U.S. airlines are so concerned about glitches in the latest version of the flight management software for Boeing’s 737 Max aircraft that they have actively avoided installing it for years, preferring instead to rely on an earlier version rolled out nearly a decade ago, people familiar with the matter told The Air Current.
The aircraft’s software issues have made headlines over the past week as the Federal Aviation Administration conducted a safety review of a bug that can arise during missed landing approaches. That created a last-minute hitch for certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10 and uncertainty around the first delivery of the Max 7, both of which rely on the latest software versions.
The FAA on Friday convened a corrective action review board (CARB) and determined that the vertical navigation (VNAV) glitch, which first surfaced in operation with WestJet in November 2024, did not represent a safety risk “because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous,” according to a statement by the agency.
But U.S. airlines have long been aware of other anomalies plaguing the fourth major software update of the 737’s flight management system (FMS) since the 1997 introduction of the 737-700, developed for Boeing by GE Aerospace3. Found in versions U14, U14.1 or both, they range from loss of capabilities to crew distractions during critical phases of flight. One of them was identified as a contributing factor in a 2022 incident where a United Airlines crew landed on the wrong runway, spawning a National Transportation Safety Board investigation. The airline later decided to roll back from the latest versions of the software.
Related: Boeing faces potential 737 Max 10 delay as FAA reviews software issue
Software bugs are not uncommon in commercial aircraft from all manufacturers. But taken together, the multitude of issues plaguing the 737’s software exemplifies the complex technical and operational deliberations and high tensions among Boeing, GE, airlines and the FAA — all under the long shadow of the 737 Max’s twin crashes in 2018 and 2019 that killed 346 people.
The Friday determination by the CARB should clear the 737-7 to be delivered at year’s end and the 737-10 to be certified in the coming days, as neither will be dependent on GE and Boeing completing a clean iteration of the software expected in 2028. TAC understands that while much of the approval process for software updates is internal to delegated engineers at Boeing and GE, the FAA has significantly stepped up its oversight of the development process of the next version, known as U14.2.
Meanwhile, U.S. airlines flying the already-certified 737 Max 8 and 9 models have avoided upgrading to U14 and U14.1. United Airlines chose to downgrade, instead sticking with the older version of the FMS software, U13, that was introduced when the first 737 Max model was certified in 2017. While that version also has a known bug that is considered by the FAA to be a low-risk safety issue and will eventually require an airworthiness directive, airlines see it as less problematic than the host of issues that were introduced with U14.
“Operators of 737 airplanes can continue safe operations with all approved versions of the 737 Flight Management Computer software,” a Boeing spokesman said in an emailed statement to TAC. “We will continue to follow the lead of the FAA as our engineers work on the next software update.”
“Safety is our top priority. We are working closely with Boeing and will support the FAA’s evaluation,” a spokesman for GE Aerospace said in an emailed statement prior to the CARB’s Friday determination.
Safely managing the workload
The FMS is an aircraft’s operating system, managing each flight by constantly calculating its performance and route while abiding by constraints from published procedures, airline limits and crew selections. Though it is involved in all phases of flight, the FMS is considered to be essential — rather than critical — flight hardware, as cockpit philosophy dictates that pilots should be able to fly the aircraft without relying on automation. However, the FMS is intertwined with the human factors that result from the workload pilots face as they manage the flight in normal and abnormal operations.
A June 2022 incident aboard a United Airlines 737 Max 9 in which the aircraft landed on the wrong parallel runway at Pittsburgh International Airport was principally traced to the crew’s misidentification of the runway. However, the NTSB noted in its probable cause statement that a dual reset of the aircraft flight management computer displays contributed to distracting the crew while on final approach.
According to the NTSB’s final report on the incident, in which there were no injuries or damage to the aircraft, the FMS screen blanking and subsequent reset was traced to a problem introduced with the U14 version of the software “due to refinements made to the earth model.”
The board noted that the fault was reproduced in the lab and was not present in either U13 or U14.1, the latter of which had begun delivering on new airplanes earlier in 2022. Boeing had sent a service letter to operators related to the dual resets in February 2020.
That bug has since been fixed with U14.1 and is unrelated to the VNAV glitch that surfaced in 2024 and made headlines this week. But both software issues share a common concern in leading to flight crew distractions and increased workload during critical phases of flight.
“The issue that we’re looking at is the workload component,” FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford told reporters on Monday regarding the VNAV issue. As part of the CARB evaluation, FAA said test pilots flew missed approach procedures in a simulator to directly experience the anomaly.
VNAV, as its name suggests, manages the aircraft’s altitude with pre-programmed levels to be achieved at a given position, significantly reducing the workload for pilots to cross their preset waypoints compared to other, simpler autopilot pitch modes. The automation directs the aircraft to climb, descend and level off in accordance with those selected constraints, including during a missed approach if a crew opts not to complete a landing.
When a pilot alters their preprogrammed, published flight path following a missed approach, the FMC may transition from VNAV to a simpler level of automation for pitch control, according to Boeing.
One 737-rated airline pilot said this scenario is more common than being instructed by a controller to fly the missed approach procedure as published.
While the precise method of handling the bug in-flight has not been detailed by Boeing publicly, a person familiar with the issue tells TAC that one mitigation is a multi-step process to allow VNAV to reengage. Pilots are instructed to clear the active route in the computer, “down-select” then “up-select” the flight’s origin airport to remove all waypoints on the route and legs pages as well as the destination airport. Crews then re-enter the destination airport and select an approach procedure before reactivating the route and flying another approach using the LNAV and VNAV autopilot modes per normal airline operations.
“That’s a little bit dicey,” said one person familiar with the procedure, noting that it is “probably doable, but has to be trained.” Boeing prior to the public disclosure of the glitch asked operators to download flight data from flights where crews believed this bug manifested, and said it is working with airlines to formalize a procedure for addressing it in flight. That process may also include using a secondary option within the computer to duplicate a flight plan as a fallback should the VNAV glitch surface.
Boeing plans to issue a bulletin to airlines about how to recognize the bug if it should occur. The FAA said it will follow with its own Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin to both U.S. airlines and foreign regulators to ensure they’re aware of Boeing’s guidance.
It’s not yet clear how much training will be required to ensure pilots can safely manage the VNAV bug, should it be seen in service. Although a missed approach is already a high-workload situation, learning how to reset the flight plan in the middle of it could necessitate as little additional training as an e-learning and interactive FMS tutorial. With the CARB’s determination that the bug does not constitute a safety issue, it’s unlikely that a time-consuming simulator session will be required to prepare pilots.
Southwest, which requires all 12,000 of its pilots to be able to fly all versions of the 737s, told TAC in an emailed statement that it “remains in close contact with the Federal Aviation Administration and Boeing. We appreciate the Safety panel’s review and will work closely with our regulator and the manufacturer to ensure the airline is taking the appropriate steps to address this issue.”
The company expects to have the Max 7, which was certified with U14, delivered at year end and in service starting around spring 2027 and badly needs the model in order to accelerate retirements of aging 737-700s.
American Airlines and Alaska Airlines, both operators of the 737 Max, said that none of their single-aisle jets were running U14 or U14.1. Delta, which is a Max 10 customer, referred all questions to Boeing.
A history of hiccups
Version U13 of the FMS software adapted version U12 from the Next Generation 737 for the latest generation of the single-aisle. Version U14 has been in operation since 2020. It principally added optimizations for vertical navigation that took into account winds and temperatures aloft, as well as enabling future air navigation system (FANS)-2 datalink communications primarily

articles.full_text:
Key Points
- Seven oil and energy stocks to watch are ExxonMobil, Chevron, Valero Energy, Marathon Petroleum, Cheniere Energy, ConocoPhillips, and Shell, selected for having the highest recent dollar trading volume among oil stocks.
- The companies span the energy value chain, including exploration and production, refining, transportation, LNG infrastructure, petrochemicals, renewable fuels, and energy marketing.
- Investor interest in these stocks may be influenced by crude oil prices, global energy demand, production costs, regulation, and company-specific performance.

ExxonMobil, Chevron, Valero Energy, Marathon Petroleum, Cheniere Energy, ConocoPhillips, and Shell are the seven Oil stocks to watch today, according to MarketBeat's stock screener tool. Oil stocks are shares of publicly traded companies involved in the exploration, production, refining, transportation, or sale of oil and related energy products. Their value can be influenced by crude oil prices, production costs, company performance, government regulations, and global energy demand. These companies had the highest dollar trading volume of any Oil stocks within the last several days.
ExxonMobil (XOM)
ExxonMobil Corporation engages in the exploration and production of crude oil and natural gas in the United States and internationally. It operates through Upstream, Energy Products, Chemical Products, and Specialty Products segments. The Upstream segment explores for and produces crude oil and natural gas.
Chevron (CVX)
Chevron Corporation, through its subsidiaries, engages in the integrated energy and chemicals operations in the United States and internationally. The company operates in two segments, Upstream and Downstream. The Upstream segment is involved in the exploration, development, production, and transportation of crude oil and natural gas; processing, liquefaction, transportation, and regasification of liquefied natural gas; transportation of crude oil through pipelines; transportation, storage, and marketing of natural gas; and carbon capture and storage, as well as a gas-to-liquids plant.
Valero Energy (VLO)
Valero Energy Corporation manufactures, markets, and sells petroleum-based and low-carbon liquid transportation fuels and petrochemical products in the United States, Canada, the United Kingdom, Ireland, Latin America, Mexico, Peru, and internationally. It operates through three segments: Refining, Renewable Diesel, and Ethanol.
Marathon Petroleum (MPC)
Marathon Petroleum Corporation, together with its subsidiaries, operates as an integrated downstream energy company primarily in the United States. The company operates through Refining & Marketing, and Midstream segments. The Refining & Marketing segment refines crude oil and other feedstocks at its refineries in the Gulf Coast, Mid-Continent, and West Coast regions of the United States; and purchases refined products and ethanol for resale and distributes refined products, including renewable diesel, through transportation, storage, distribution, and marketing services.
Cheniere Energy (LNG)
Cheniere Energy, Inc., an energy infrastructure company, primarily engages in the liquefied natural gas (LNG) related businesses in the United States. It owns and operates the Sabine Pass LNG terminal in Cameron Parish, Louisiana; and the Corpus Christi LNG terminal near Corpus Christi, Texas. The company also owns Creole Trail pipeline, a 94-mile natural gas supply pipeline that interconnects the Sabine Pass LNG Terminal with several interstate and intrastate pipelines; and operates Corpus Christi pipeline, a 21.5-mile natural gas supply pipeline that interconnects the Corpus Christi LNG terminal with various interstate and intrastate natural gas pipelines.
ConocoPhillips (COP)
ConocoPhillips explores for, produces, transports, and markets crude oil, bitumen, natural gas, liquefied natural gas (LNG), and natural gas liquids in the United States, Canada, China, Libya, Malaysia, Norway, the United Kingdom, and internationally. The company's portfolio includes unconventional plays in North America; conventional assets in North America, Europe, Asia, and Australia; global LNG developments; oil sands assets in Canada; and an inventory of global exploration prospects.
Shell (SHEL)
Shell plc operates as an energy and petrochemical company Europe, Asia, Oceania, Africa, the United States, and Rest of the Americas. The company operates through Integrated Gas, Upstream, Marketing, Chemicals and Products, and Renewables and Energy Solutions segments. articles.title: This is how the informal market in Cuba begins the day: The dollar rises and the euro also increases - CiberCuba
articles.summary: This is how the informal market in Cuba begins the day: The dollar rises and the euro also increases  CiberCuba
articles.full_text:
At 10:00 a.m., Cuban local time, opens this Saturday, October 3, 2026, with a session characterized by the rise of the dollar and the euro.
The U.S. dollar rises to 785 Cuban pesos, the euro stands at 880 CUP, and the MLC, with low trading volume, is around 468 pesos, a value that should be considered as indicative.
The upward movement of the dollar is not temporary: the US currency has experienced a sustained rise, increasing from 733 pesos a week ago to the current 785, confirming a trend that shows no signs of slowing down. The euro is also following the upward pressure, reaching a new high this month.
The United States dollar (USD)
The U.S. dollar is being quoted today at 785 Cuban pesos (CUP) in the informal market, with a buying rate at 780 CUP and a selling rate at 789 CUP. This represents an increase of 11 pesos compared to the previous day, when the currency closed around 774 CUP.
Exchange Rate Evolution
In a weekly perspective, the jump is even more striking: seven days ago, the dollar was trading at 733 pesos, which means an increase of 52 pesos, equivalent to 7.1% in just one week.
The 30-day comparison shows the current rate at 107 pesos above the 678 CUP recorded at the beginning of September, although this reference may partly reflect methodological adjustments of the index.
In the last 30 days, the dollar has fluctuated between a low of 678 and the current high of 785 CUP. The demand for dollars remains high among those seeking to protect their savings against the depreciation of the peso.
The euro (EUR)
The euro is quoted today at 880 Cuban pesos (CUP), with a buying rate of 870 CUP and a selling rate of 889 CUP. Compared to the previous trading day, when it was at 875 CUP, it shows an increase of 5 pesos, a 0.5% rise.
In the past week, the euro has risen 40 pesos from 840 CUP that it was at seven days ago, an increase of 4.8%. On the monthly horizon, the European currency has gained 106.5 pesos compared to 773 CUP from 30 days ago, although this comparison should be viewed with caution due to potential methodological adjustments.
The euro exceeds the dollar by 95 pesos, consolidating its position as the most expensive currency in the Cuban parallel market, driven by limited supply and the demand from those receiving remittances from Europe.
The MLC
The MLC appears this Saturday around 468 Cuban pesos (CUP), with a purchase price of 472 CUP and a selling price of 463 CUP. This value should be taken as indicative, as the volume of operations supporting it during this time period is limited.
Regarding the previous session, when it was at 504 CUP, it recorded a drop of 36 pesos, a decrease of 7.1%. In the last week, it has fallen 21.5 pesos from the 489 CUP of seven days ago. Without physical existence, its use is limited to state-run businesses that accept it, which restricts its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Summary of informal market rates
- Exchange rate of the dollar USD to CUP: 785 CUP
- Exchange rate of the euro EUR to CUP: 880 CUP
- Exchange rate from MLC to CUP: 468 CUP (indicative value, limited data)
The official exchange rate of the Central Bank of Cuba (Segment III), set today at 695 CUP per dollar and 783 CUP per euro, remains significantly below the rates that are applied in everyday practice in the informal currency market.
Although Segment III was introduced as a more flexible exchange mechanism, its official rate remains far removed from that of the informal market and fails to meet the actual demand for foreign currency among the population.
The gap between the two markets today reaches 90 pesos for the dollar and 97 pesos for the euro, a difference that illustrates the extent of the discrepancy between the official economy and the everyday reality of Cubans.
The gap between the official and informal rates reflects the persistent shortage of foreign currency in the state banking system and the high demand for dollars and euros from the population, whether for emigration, importing goods, protecting savings, or making purchases in the private sector.
In a scenario of sustained inflation, low state wages, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, every fluctuation in the informal market directly affects internal prices and the purchasing power of Cubans.
The Exchange Rate of CiberCuba is an index of the informal Cuban market created through the automated analysis of thousands of currency buy-sell posts in Telegram and Facebook groups; the calculation excludes atypical offers and spam messages, weighs each transaction according to its age, and consolidates a representative value that is updated several times a day.

The European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) has proposed amendments to the markets in crypto-assets regulation (MiCA) in response to the European Commission’s consultation on the framework.
The recommendations aim to simplify MiCA, strengthen investor protection and address services including decentralised finance (DeFi), staking, lending and borrowing.
ESMA has proposed a new regulated service for crypto-asset service providers (CASPs) that give clients access to DeFi protocols. It has also called for clearer criteria for when a service counts as fully decentralised, to stop operators using DeFi structures to avoid MiCA.
The regulator also wants binding rules on token classification and clarity that stablecoin-settled derivatives can still qualify as financial instruments under Mifid II.
On investor protection, ESMA has proposed stricter marketing rules, including for influencer promotion, greater cost transparency and proportionate requirements for staking, lending and borrowing, backed by mandatory disclosures.
Read more: ESMA signals end of MiCA grace period
With regards to supervision, ESMA has proposed powers to act against unauthorised third-country firms, block fraudulent websites and freeze crypto-assets, as well as a ban on regulated firms servicing stablecoins that do not comply with MiCA.
To simplify the regime, it has suggested reducing crypto white paper notification procedures, removing duplicate authorisation requirements and harmonising prudential standards.
Beyond the MiCA review, ESMA has called for a framework covering tokenised securities and on-chain settlement, including cross-border activity.
The recommendations follow the end of MiCA’s transition period on 1 July 2026. CASPs without authorisation by that date were required to wind down their activities while protecting investor interests.
In the UK, the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) opened applications for crypto-asset authorisation on 30 September. Firms must apply by 28 February 2027, ahead of the regime taking effect on 25 October 2027.

articles.title: U.S. Treasury Yields Hit 32-Year High Amid Allied Sell-Off - 조선일보
articles.summary: U.S. Treasury Yields Hit 32-Year High Amid Allied Sell-Off  조선일보
articles.full_text:
U.S. Treasury yields, which have a broad impact on global markets, recorded their largest quarterly rise in 32 years. According to the U.S. Treasury Department, the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 5.29% annually, up 0.85 percentage points from the previous quarter, at the end of the third quarter (July–September). This marks the largest increase since the first quarter of 1994. Treasury prices move inversely to yields. In 1994, when the Federal Reserve rapidly raised the benchmark interest rate without prior notice, Treasury yields surged to such an extent that the year was dubbed the "Great Bond Massacre." The current situation indicates a shock comparable to that period is unfolding in the bond market.
◇France, Japan, South Korea…Shift to Net Selling
The fundamental reason for the declining popularity of U.S. Treasuries is the massive U.S. national debt. With chronic fiscal deficits compounded by rising interest burdens due to higher Treasury yields, the U.S. federal debt has surpassed 40 trillion dollars (approximately 53,800 trillion Korean won) and continues to grow in a vicious cycle.
While demand from allied nations’ financial institutions and central banks had previously sustained purchases of U.S. Treasuries as a safe asset, this trend has recently reversed. According to U.S. "Treasury International Capital (TIC)" data as of July, foreign net purchases of U.S. Treasuries for the year totaled 246.5 billion dollars—the lowest since 2021, during the COVID-19 pandemic. Net purchases peaked at 819.7 billion dollars in 2023 but have declined for four consecutive years, shrinking to one-third of the 2023 level in the past year.
The recent shift includes not only trade-dispute-affected nations like China but also allied countries selling U.S. Treasuries. TIC data analysis shows that France was the top net seller over the three months starting in May, when yields began rising sharply. France sold 31 billion dollars worth of U.S. Treasuries, surpassing China’s 24 billion dollars in net sales. In the same period last year, France was the second-largest net buyer after the U.K., but the situation reversed within a year.
Japan and South Korea, which had been major net buyers of U.S. Treasuries, also became net sellers in recent months, ranking third and fourth (excluding hedge fund hubs like the Cayman Islands and the UAE). While they had net purchases of 13.5 billion dollars and 9.1 billion dollars, respectively, from May to July last year, this year they recorded net sales of 15.4 billion dollars and 5.1 billion dollars. Norway and Taiwan, which had been net buyers last year, also sold 2.8 billion dollars and 1.4 billion dollars, respectively, joining the list of allied net sellers.
◇Hedge Funds Fill Void Left by Long-Term Investors
The shift to net selling by countries that once heavily bought U.S. Treasuries stems from distrust in the U.S.’s massive national debt and growing fiscal deficits. This has been compounded by individual countries’ circumstances forcing them to sell. In France, where most foreign reserves are held in gold, central bank sales were minimal, but private financial institutions sold significant amounts of U.S. Treasuries. This is attributed to private institutions, rather than state entities, selling en masse to hedge against further rate hikes.
Japan and South Korea’s sales were driven by efforts to defend against high exchange rates in the first half of the year. To secure dollar "ammunition" for forex market interventions amid heightened volatility, both countries sold U.S. Treasuries. Japan’s dollar-denominated foreign reserves decreased from 1.2 trillion dollars in April to 1.1 trillion dollars in July. South Korea’s authorities announced injecting 9.6 billion dollars in the second quarter to counter high exchange rates. Taiwan’s central bank also sold U.S. Treasuries to address currency appreciation. However, recent exchange rate declines may reverse this trend.
Norway’s sovereign wealth fund, the world’s largest, announced plans to reduce its reliance on U.S. Treasuries as part of portfolio diversification, increasing the likelihood of further sales. The fund declared in early August that it would lower its government bond allocation from 70% to 50% and increase investments in corporate bonds, initiating asset adjustments.
The void left by stable investors like insurers and central banks is being filled by hedge funds, which engage in short-term trading. A June report by Federal Reserve economist Philip Monin revealed that hedge funds held approximately 4 trillion dollars in U.S. Treasuries as of September last year, accounting for 8.5% of the market—double the 2023 level. The report noted, "The increased share held by hedge funds amplifies market instability."
◇Rate Hike Boomerang: "New Trigger Is France"
Rising U.S. Treasury yields have spilled over into global financial market instability, creating a vicious cycle that pushes up bond yields in countries that sold Treasuries. France is a prime example. Amid growing fiscal deficits and political turmoil ahead of its April 2025 presidential election, France’s 10-year bond yield surpassed 5% on the 2nd, the highest since July 2002.
The French Treasury’s announcement to borrow a record 340 billion euros next year to address fiscal deficits has also fueled distrust in French bonds. Bloomberg stated, "The recent surge in U.S. Treasury yields has exposed France’s weak fiscal health. Instability in France, a eurozone member, risks spreading across Europe."
Japan and South Korea face rapid rises in bond yields due to central bank rate hikes to combat inflation. Japan’s 10-year bond yield exceeded 3% in September for the first time in 30 years and surpassed 3.1% earlier this month. South Korea’s 10-year bond yield hit 4.6% last month—the highest since October 2022—and remains near 4.4%, the highest in four years. South Korean loan rates have also risen, with new mortgage rates averaging 4.4% in August, the highest in three years and nine months.
◇"If AI Optimism Fades, Stock Market Shock Looms"
Rising bond yields typically increase funding costs for investors and corporations, reduce the appeal of stocks relative to bonds, and trigger stock declines. However, the stock market impact remains limited so far, as funds continue flowing into equities driven by AI optimism despite fears of further yield increases.
Some experts warn that if AI optimism wanes, the "shadow" of high bond yields could crash stock markets. Barclays’ recent report stated, "Amid overlapping shocks, private-sector-led AI is driving massive demand and growth. However, if AI expectations fail to materialize or take longer than anticipated, the market’s optimism could abruptly adjust, leading to a sharp deterioration in investment sentiment and a major shock."

Summary
- Market moving news for Asian trading on Monday, October 5, 2026.
- US dollar firms, EUR/USD hits its lowest since May 2025 and oil edges lower as Gulf supply recovers, while Japan's Nikkei hits a three-month high on AI-related stocks.
Summary:
- Oil edged lower to open the week as recovering Middle East exports and a G7 stock release offset Houthi claims of attacks on Aramco sites.
- Saudi Aramco unexpectedly cut November prices to Asia to the widest discount since 2020, and OPEC+ held output steady.
- The US dollar rose against majors and EUR/USD fell to its lowest since May 2025. USD/JPY held near 157 despite firmer rhetoric from Tokyo.
- The BOJ's Uchida called AI a big demand shock, and Japan's services PMI showed intense price pressure. The Nikkei hit a three-month high.
- Australia's services PMI eased as job cuts returned, Chalmers called the Iran war an economic disaster, and New Zealand export prices rose.
- Deutsche Bank says gold is oversold. The Fed minutes on Wednesday will test the "one more hike" guidance.
Oil and geopolitics
Oil futures edged slightly lower to start the week. Rising Middle East exports and a 100 million barrel emergency stock release by G7 nations offset fresh attacks on Gulf energy infrastructure. Yemen's Houthis claimed missile and drone strikes on Saudi Aramco facilities in Riyadh and Khurais, which Saudi Arabia has not confirmed.
Saudi Aramco unexpectedly cut its November Arab Light price for Asia by $3, to $5 below the Oman/Dubai benchmark. That's the widest discount since June 2020, against expectations of a hike, and Aramco raised prices for Europe at the same time. OPEC+ kept November output targets unchanged, and a capacity review key to 2027 quotas has slipped to mid-November.
On the diplomatic front, Iran's parliament speaker reportedly said Tehran would reject new US peace proposals and keep the Strait of Hormuz shut until its conditions are met. Those comments could not be independently verified. The US has also withdrawn all its B-1 bombers from Britain's RAF Fairford after a suspected Iran-linked plot against the base.
FX
The US dollar firmed against major currencies, with EUR/USD sliding to its lowest since May 2025 amid French bond market stress and reports that Spanish government officials are preparing for an early election. MUFG recommended a new short EUR/JPY trade, citing euro-area fragmentation risk and expectations of further Bank of Japan tightening.
USD/JPY held near 158 despite a shift in tone from Tokyo. Economy Minister Kiuchi said on Friday that Japan was no longer in deflation. Finance Minister Katayama, also back on Friday, said the government was not reflationist and stood ready with the US to act against excessive volatility.
Japan
BOJ Deputy Governor Uchida described artificial intelligence as a large positive demand shock that has lifted prices and eased financial conditions, while warning of correction risk if profits fail to follow. Japan's services PMI eased to 51.3, but hiring accelerated and output prices rose sharply, and S&P Global said the BOJ could hike as soon as October. The Nikkei jumped around 2.5% to a three-month high by midday, led by AI-related stocks, as equities across the region firmed.
Australia and New Zealand
Australia's services PMI eased to 51.9 as firms cut staff and price pressures intensified, with S&P Global saying that could keep the Reserve Bank leaning hawkish. Treasurer Jim Chalmers called the Iran war an economic disaster and warned rising bond yields would add billions to debt servicing costs. ANZ's commodity price index for New Zealand rose 0.6% in September on higher oil and gas prices, and a weaker kiwi lifted local-currency returns by 2.8%.
Ahead mid-week
Minutes of the Federal Reserve's September meeting are due on Wednesday. They will show how firmly officials back their guidance for one more hike, after softer US jobs and inflation data trimmed October hike bets.

articles.summary: WTI drops to near $89.00 as OPEC+ holds November targets  FXStreet
articles.full_text:
West Texas Intermediate (WTI) oil price extends its losses for the second successive day, trading around $89.30 during Asian hours on Monday. Crude oil prices experienced a decline after G7 nations agreed to release 100 million barrels of crude and diesel from emergency reserves, pledging to avoid energy export restrictions following pressure from US President Donald Trump. Despite the ongoing conflict, regional crude exports briefly spiked above pre-war levels in late September, reaching peak flows of up to 22.5 million barrels per day according to data from Kpler. This compares to a pre-war average of 18 million barrels per day recorded between March 2025 and February.
Moreover, Oil prices fall due to an agreement by the Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries and its allies (OPEC+) to maintain steady production targets for November. The decision aligned with widespread market expectations that further adjustments to output policy would be deferred until next year.
Key producers, including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Iraq, Kuwait, Algeria, Kazakhstan, and Oman, continue to pump well below their designated quotas, with overall exports running at just 60% to 80% of normal volumes due to ongoing export disruptions linked to the conflict involving the US, Israel, and Iran.
Geopolitical instability in the region escalated as Saudi-backed forces in Yemen launched a major military offensive to reclaim territory from Houthi forces. The action followed weeks of heightened tensions, during which the Iran-backed group captured the strategic Bab el-Mandeb strait. This key maritime passage between the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden had been serving as a critical alternative bypass for Saudi oil shipments looking to avoid the Strait of Hormuz.
Brent eases as supply fears fade, but Middle East risks linger
Analysts at Rabobank note that Brent crude prices have “retreated last week as improved Hormuz flows and the partial restoration of Saudi Arabia’s East-West pipeline eased supply concerns,” highlighting a tentative normalization in physical market conditions. However, they caution that “the deployment of another aircraft carrier to the Middle East threatens to disrupt the recent recovery,” underscoring that geopolitical risk remains a key potential brake on the recent pullback in prices.
WTI Oil FAQs
WTI Oil is a type of Crude Oil sold on international markets. The WTI stands for West Texas Intermediate, one of three major types including Brent and Dubai Crude. WTI is also referred to as “light” and “sweet” because of its relatively low gravity and sulfur content respectively. It is considered a high quality Oil that is easily refined. It is sourced in the United States and distributed via the Cushing hub, which is considered “The Pipeline Crossroads of the World”. It is a benchmark for the Oil market and WTI price is frequently quoted in the media.
Like all assets, supply and demand are the key drivers of WTI Oil price. As such, global growth can be a driver of increased demand and vice versa for weak global growth. Political instability, wars, and sanctions can disrupt supply and impact prices. The decisions of OPEC, a group of major Oil-producing countries, is another key driver of price. The value of the US Dollar influences the price of WTI Crude Oil, since Oil is predominantly traded in US Dollars, thus a weaker US Dollar can make Oil more affordable and vice versa.
The weekly Oil inventory reports published by the American Petroleum Institute (API) and the Energy Information Agency (EIA) impact the price of WTI Oil. Changes in inventories reflect fluctuating supply and demand. If the data shows a drop in inventories it can indicate increased demand, pushing up Oil price. Higher inventories can reflect increased supply, pushing down prices. API’s report is published every Tuesday and EIA’s the day after. Their results are usually similar, falling within 1% of each other 75% of the time. The EIA data is considered more reliable, since it is a government agency.
OPEC (Organization of the Petroleum Exporting Countries) is a group of 12 Oil-producing nations who collectively decide production quotas for member countries at twice-yearly meetings. Their decisions often impact WTI Oil prices. When OPEC decides to lower quotas, it can tighten supply, pushing up Oil prices. When OPEC increases production, it has the opposite effect. OPEC+ refers to an expanded group that includes ten extra non-OPEC members, the most notable of which is Russia.

articles.summary: Asia-Pac Equities Begin Week Higher As Softer US Jobs Data Shifts Fed Expectations  Sahi
articles.full_text:
Global stock markets reacted positively to a cooling U.S. labor market. September nonfarm payrolls grew by just 29,000, far below the consensus estimate of 90,000. This disappointing print has prompted traders to dial back expectations of an October interest rate hike, setting up a near-term global equity relief rally.
Market snapshot: Asia-Pacific equity markets started the week on a positive note following a strong Friday session on Wall Street. This upward momentum was triggered by disappointing U.S. employment data, which significantly reduced expectations for a near-term interest rate hike by the Federal Reserve. The raw input alert noted movements of ASX 200 (+0.39%) and Nikkei 226 (+2.56%) (as stated in the source alert; not independently verified), reflecting positive sentiment at the open.
Data Snapshot
- U.S. nonfarm payrolls added only 29,000 jobs in September, far below the 90,000 expected by economists.
- The U.S. unemployment rate rose to 4.2% in September from 4.1% in August.
- Expectations for an October Fed rate hike fell to 17%, down from over 25% prior to the jobs report.
What's Changed
- U.S. September payroll growth slowed to 29,000 from a revised 133,000 in August.
- The probability of a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in October fell to 17% from approximately 28% prior to the report.
- The U.S. unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1% in August.
Key Takeaways
- Sharp slowdown in hiring: The addition of 29,000 jobs in September was a significant drop from the revised 133,000 in August, underscoring a cooling labor market.
- Interest rate relief: The weak print led traders to price in an 83% probability of the Federal Reserve holding interest rates steady at its October meeting.
- Equity market boost: Global stocks reacted positively to the prospect of a pause in the Fed's aggressive monetary tightening cycle.
- Thin holiday trading: Gains in the Asia-Pacific region occurred amidst thin trading volumes, with markets in South Korea and China closed for national holidays.
SAHI Perspective
The dramatic deceleration in U.S. hiring is a clear sign that previous interest rate hikes are cooling the real economy. By adding just 29,000 jobs in September, the U.S. labor market has shifted to what economists call a 'low-hire, low-fire' environment. This gives the Federal Reserve substantial breathing room to pause rate increases in October. However, the persistence of energy-driven inflation from the ongoing Middle East tensions means the Fed's inflation fight is not entirely over, and a rate hike in December remains a strong possibility.
Market Implications
For Indian and emerging markets, a pause in the Federal Reserve's rate hike cycle is highly positive. It eases pressure on local currencies, such as the Indian Rupee, and reduces the risk of aggressive capital outflows. However, persistent global uncertainties, including elevated crude oil prices and high U.S. Treasury yields, may continue to act as a cap on major equity gains.
Trading Signals
Market Bias: Bullish
Weaker-than-expected September hiring of 29,000 jobs has reduced the probability of an October Fed rate hike to 17%, boosting global equity sentiment.
Overweight: Technology, Commodities
Underweight: Financials
Trigger Factors:
- U.S. Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation print scheduled for October 14, 2026
- Movement in the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield below the 5.2% mark
- Upcoming corporate earnings reports for the current quarter
Time Horizon: Near-term (0-3 months)
Industry Context
The global labor market is exhibiting a stark divergence. While healthcare and construction sectors continue to add positions (healthcare added 17,000 jobs and construction added 11,000 in September), white-collar sectors like financial services are pulling back. This uneven hiring trend suggests that while some parts of the economy remain resilient, other sectors are starting to feel the pinch of high borrowing costs.
Key Risks to Watch
- Sticky inflation: High energy costs driven by geopolitical conflicts in the Middle East could force the Fed to resume hikes later in the year.
- Slowing economic growth: If the labor market cools too rapidly, fears of a deeper economic slowdown or recession could override the positive sentiment from rate pauses.
- Elevated bond yields: Despite easing rate expectations, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield remains elevated near 5.26%, continuing to pressure stock valuations.
Recent Developments
U.S. nonfarm payrolls rose only 29,000 in September, cutting October Fed rate hike odds to ~17% and lifting global equities. The U.S. unemployment rate edged up to 4.2% from 4.1% in August, while job additions for July and August were revised downwards by a combined 60,000 jobs.
Closing Insight
The sharp cooling in the U.S. labor market has provided global stock markets with a much-needed reprieve by taking a near-term Federal Reserve interest rate hike off the table. However, with inflation pressures still lingering from geopolitical disruptions, investors must remain vigilant and monitor upcoming inflation checkpoints.

articles.title: Cuba's Informal Currency Market Wraps Up: Dollar Holds Steady While Euro Dips - CubaHeadlines
articles.summary: Cuba's Informal Currency Market Wraps Up: Dollar Holds Steady While Euro Dips  CubaHeadlines
articles.full_text:
As of 8:00 PM local time in Cuba, the informal currency exchange market concluded its session on Sunday, October 4, 2026, displaying mixed trends: the U.S. dollar remained unchanged, whereas the euro saw a slight dip compared to its opening rate. Meanwhile, the MLC provided a tentative rate that should be approached cautiously due to limited data availability during this time.
U.S. Dollar Analysis
The U.S. dollar (USD) closed the day at 785 Cuban pesos (CUP), holding steady from the previous day when it also ended at 785 pesos. Over the week, however, there has been a noticeable upward trend, with the dollar rising from 740 pesos a week ago, marking a 45-peso increase (+6.1%). Looking at the past month, the dollar has surged by 102.5 pesos from 683 pesos, reflecting a significant rise of +15%, though this may partly be due to methodological adjustments in the index. The demand for dollars remains high among those seeking to safeguard their savings against the peso's depreciation.
Euro's Market Movement
The euro (EUR) ended the session at 879 Cuban pesos (CUP), reflecting a decrease of 6.5 pesos from 885 pesos the previous day (-0.7%). Despite this brief decline, the European currency maintains an upward weekly trend, having increased from 847 pesos a week ago, gaining 31.5 pesos (+3.7%). Over the month, the euro has risen by 103.5 pesos from 775 pesos, a 13.4% increase, though these figures should be interpreted with care as they may include methodological adjustments. The euro remains 94 pesos above the dollar, reinforcing its dominant position in Cuba's parallel market.
MLC Exchange Rate Insights
The MLC is approximately valued at 532 Cuban pesos (CUP), but this rate is merely indicative due to the scarcity and unreliability of available data at closing. Compared to the previous session's 460 pesos, there appears to be a +72 pesos variation (+15.7%), which likely reflects sample irregularities rather than actual market movements. A week ago, the MLC was at 542 pesos, and 30 days ago, it stood at 462 pesos. Without physical presence, its use is confined to state-run stores that accept it, limiting its circulation compared to cash currencies.
Summary of Exchange Rates as of October 4, 2026
USD to CUP exchange rate: 785 CUP. EUR to CUP exchange rate: 879 CUP. MLC to CUP exchange rate: 532 CUP (indicative, limited data). The official Central Bank of Cuba rate (Segment III), at 695 CUP per dollar and 783 CUP per euro, remains significantly lower than the rates observed in the informal market.
Although Segment III was introduced as a more flexible exchange mechanism, its official rate lags far behind the informal market and fails to meet the population's real currency demands. Over the past month, the official dollar rate increased from 638 to 695 CUP, and the euro from 742 to 783 CUP, showing an upward trend that still doesn't bridge the gap with the parallel market: the informal dollar exceeds the official rate by 90 pesos, and the euro by 96 pesos.
Impact on Cuban Economy
In a setting characterized by persistent inflation, low state wages, and increasing partial dollarization of the economy, fluctuations in the informal market directly affect domestic prices and Cubans' purchasing power.
The informal currency market in Cuba operates independently of state financial institutions, relying on private buying and selling networks. Although the Cuban regime does not officially acknowledge it, this market effectively determines Cubans' real purchasing power.
The CiberCuba Exchange Rate is an index of Cuba's informal market, derived from automated analysis of thousands of currency trading posts on Telegram and Facebook groups. It filters out unusual offers and spam, weighing each transaction by its recency to produce a representative value that is updated multiple times daily.
Currency Equivalences

- 5 USD = 3,925 CUP
- 10 USD = 7,850 CUP

- 100 USD = 78,500 CUP
Euro (EUR) to Cuban Peso (CUP) Equivalences, as of Sunday, October 4, 2026:
- 1 EUR = 879 CUP

- 10 EUR = 8,790 CUP
- 20 EUR = 17,580 CUP
- 50 EUR = 43,950 CUP
- 100 EUR = 87,900 CUP

Frequently Asked Questions about Cuba's Informal Currency Market
Why is the informal market significant in Cuba?
The informal market in Cuba is significant because it operates independently of state control and effectively sets the real exchange rates that influence Cuban purchasing power and economic conditions.
How does the CiberCuba Exchange Rate work?
The CiberCuba Exchange Rate is calculated by analyzing thousands of currency trading posts on social media, filtering out anomalies, and weighing transactions to provide a representative and regularly updated value.
What impact does the informal market have on Cuban prices?
Fluctuations in the informal market can directly affect internal prices and the purchasing power of Cubans, especially in an economy with high inflation and low state salaries.
